core.title: The divine within every life
core.text: Bhagavad Gita 10.20 presents the divine as the Self abiding in all beings. Verse 18.61 describes the Lord within every heart and beings moving through maya as if on a machine. These deepen the connection with Uday’s account of life experienced from within a design, without stating his entire game formulation.

traditionsIntro: Readers can explore divine presence, unity, dignity, and interdependence through their own traditions. These are specific points of comparison, not a claim that every religion teaches that we designed and entered the same game.

traditions.title: Christianity: life in God and unity
traditions.text: Acts 17.28 describes life, movement, and existence in God. John 17.21 expresses Jesus’s prayer for unity among his followers in the Father and Son. These offer connections with divine presence and relationship; neither passage says that every person designed the universe.

traditions.title: Islam: divine nearness
traditions.text: Quran 50.16 describes God’s knowledge of human inward life and profound nearness. Quran 42.11 affirms God’s incomparability. These passages invite reflection on nearness while preserving the distinction between God and creation; they do not declare that humans are Allah.

traditions.title: Judaism: the divine image and human dignity
traditions.text: Genesis 1.27 describes humanity as created in the divine image. This provides a point of connection with dignity shared across human lives. Being created in God’s image is different from claiming that a human personality is the Creator.

traditions.title: Sikh tradition: one light within all
traditions.text: Guru Nanak’s hymn on Ang 13 of the Guru Granth Sahib describes the one divine light shining within all and becoming manifest through the Guru’s teaching. This closely connects with Uday’s emphasis on recognizing the same source in other people. The passage does not establish his complete predesigned-game account.

traditions.title: Buddhism: understanding conditions
traditions.text: Samyutta Nikaya 12.20 explains dependent arising: experiences arise through conditions and can cease. It offers a connection with examining experience and its relationships. This teaching does not assert a shared creator Self or a universe designed before entry; its difference is part of the comparison.

healthIntro: Uday interprets illness and its timing within the design. The sources below distinguish Ayurvedic explanations, astrological associations, and population research. They do not establish a birth chart as a medical diagnosis or an exact forecast of disease onset. Illness is not evidence of failed realization; seek appropriate medical care.

health.title: Ayurveda: time is one factor among several
health.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana 11.43, lists unsuitable sensory contact, errors of judgment, and time or seasonal change among disease causes. This supports a traditional relationship between time and health. It does not reduce every illness to planetary positions at birth.

health.title: Medical astrology: documented traditional associations
health.text: Brihat Jataka 23.7 connects planetary configurations with forms of illness. This establishes that such associations occur in classical astrology. A textual prediction is different from clinical confirmation: this passage does not demonstrate diagnostic accuracy or reliably establish when a particular person will become ill.

health.title: Birth season and health: what studies measure
health.text: A 2015 study of 1,749,400 medical records found associations between birth month and 55 disease categories. It discussed seasonal influences during early development. A later study found that results varied across populations and locations. These associations do not establish planetary causation, determine an individual’s destiny, or predict an exact illness date.
